claims.claim: The Lucas-Lehmer criterion has both directions proved for an odd prime exponent.
The recurrence begins with4 and requires q-2 iterations.
For q=3, the first iterate is0 modulo7.
Reduction modulo2^q-1 and the previously checked4.3.2 method preserve the test.
The companion-matrix identity gives the U recurrence and V trace.
Equation29 follows from the matrix identity.
The closed form for U in equation30 follows from the characteristic roots.
The closed form for V in equation31 follows from the characteristic roots.
The addition formula in equation32 holds for the stated indices.
Equation33 lifts a zero modulo p^e to a zero at index np modulo p^(e+1), including p=2 and e=1.
The displayed doubling congruence for U_2n is valid modulo p^(e+1).
The displayed congruence for U_(2n+1) is a^2 modulo p^(e+1).
The triple-index congruences follow by the same matrix binomial expansion.
The general k-index congruences have coefficient k*a^(k-1) and a^k.
The odd and even binomial expansions in34 reproduce U and V.
For odd p, equation35 gives U_p=3^((p-1)/2) and V_p=4 modulo p.
The two signs of U_p imply a zero at p+epsilon when p does not divide6.
The special primes2 and3 in equation36 are covered directly by U_2=4 and U_3=15.
Invertibility of the companion matrix ensures existence of a positive zero index modulo every N.
Equation37 follows because scalar powers form exactly the multiples of the least index.
Consecutive U terms are coprime and the shifted sequence is an invertible scalar multiple of the initial sequence.
The doubled V identity yields equation38 for L_n.
The common divisor of U_n and V_n divides2.
Vanishing L_(q-2) forces the U rank to be exactly2^(q-1).
Every prime divisor of2^q-1 is greater than3.
The rank divides the least common multiple of the prime-power rank bounds.
The common even factors bound that lcm by the product divided by2^(r-1).
The displayed inequality chain forces at most two prime divisors and an lcm equal to m or2m.
A power-of-two lcm forces all prime multiplicities to be one.
The two possible prime factors must have opposite signs in2^k±1.
The identity (2^k+1)(2^h-1)=2^q-1 forces k=h and q even, contradicting the hypothesis.
For prime2^q-1, the square-root-of-alpha construction has norm-1.
The doubled identity and primality give V_(2^(q-2))=0.

claims.claim: The number2^D-1 is divisible by every odd p with p-1 dividing D.
E=lcm(1,...,1000) is the product of the maximal prime powers within the bound.
The first-stage powering computes a^E modulo N.
The second-stage condition p-1 dividing E*q gives divisibility, not automatically a proper factor.
The stated factor p has the displayed factorization of p-1, with its large factor41231.
For the book example,428 divides E and base2 gives A=1 modulo the whole input.
Both factors of the reduced n6 have base-two order428, so no choice of exponent separates them.
The saved base-three witness gives the promised proper factor with the same bounds.
Multiplication by an invertible A^k preserves the gcd in the batched formula.
The inclusive33<=r<=3334 batches cover all9424 required primes.
The alternate4,2 increments cover the required primes without asserting primality of every candidate exponent.
Splitting a gcd=N batch can help in general but cannot repair A=1.
With a random unit and the added two-adic ladder, the failure probability per base is at most one half.
Repeated prime factors do not invalidate separation modulo two distinct primes.
Perfect prime powers and nonunit bases have explicit preliminary branches.
The ladder uses logarithmically many extra stages rather than independent full powering at every stage.
Lucas V polynomials have the stated composition and doubling identities over every modulus.
Binary evaluation of a consecutive V pair takes O(log m) modular operations.
A nonsquare discriminant gives a norm-one root whose order divides p+1.
A nonzero square discriminant gives the corresponding p-1 bound.
Composition computes V_E and the second stage tests V_q(V_E)-2.
The explicit finite product provides a nonzero integer divisible by all eligible odd primes.
The parameter distribution and the extra ladder give the recorded positive success bound under the stated model.
Divisibility by p is kept distinct from a proper gcd of the full N.
The Jacobi product definition is well-defined with multiplicities.
Zero, one, periodicity and numerator multiplicativity follow componentwise.
Gauss's lemma gives the supplementary law for2.
Multiplying prime reciprocity gives the stated law for odd composite arguments.
The convention J(a,1)=1 is needed for termination and arguments equal to1.
The reciprocity algorithm preserves a signed-symbol invariant and terminates by Euclidean descent.
Its division count is logarithmic and classical amortization gives quadratic bit complexity.
The accepted Solovay-Strassen units form a subgroup.
A repeated prime divisor prevents that subgroup from being the whole unit group.
For a squarefree composite, a nonresidue in one CRT component and1 in another gives a rejecting unit.
The subgroup index proves the one-half bound for each fixed composite input.
Prime inputs are always accepted; the fixed-input error bound is not a posterior probability.
The number of roots of x^u=1 is the product of gcd(u,p_i-1), with no extra prime-power multiplicity.
The Jacobi character on those roots is nontrivial precisely in the recorded same-index case.
The x^u=-1 roots exist precisely when all required two-adic inequalities hold.
The parity of the minimal two-adic components fixes the sign of those roots.
The three branches delta=2,1/2,1 give the printed Monier formula.
Repeated prime factors cannot give a false-acceptance probability above one quarter.
In the squarefree case, probability above one quarter requires a Carmichael number and the stated valuations.
The1729 example has648 accepted bases and probability3/8.
Every strong-test accepted base is also a Solovay-Strassen accepted base.
The strict strength comparison is consistent with the saved examples; no new census is run.
Lebesgue1847 ends at517, not520; this is the second occurrence of C0129.
The extended test permits zero residues so a fixed multiple of a prime is not a false rejection.
The matrix uses N-1 columns and excludes the undefined input1.
The corrected remainder count retains -1 and min(b,r), giving at least half ones in every row.
The printed intermediate bound fails for n=9,N=12; C0156 preserves the final existence theorem.
Averaging selects a column rejecting at least half of the remaining composite rows.
Removing that column preserves the necessary count in surviving rows.
At most floor(lg N) columns eliminate every row.
The proof is nonuniform existence, not an efficient construction of the bases.
The lcm and union bound construct each finite block for a single infinite sequence.
Adding multiples of the lcm makes all bases strictly increasing without changing their tests.
The concatenated block lengths give floor(lg n)*(floor(lg n)-1)/2 tests.
The O(log n) single-infinite-sequence addendum is not solved.

Each horizontal complex integral converges absolutely and conjugate roots contribute conjugate integrals.

The Mellin identity follows from the absolutely convergent Euler product.
Converting li to an integral from2 gives C=li(2)-log2.
The series for C cancels the first exponential-integral term.
All40 printed decimal places of C have a saved interval certificate.
The positive tail R has its E1 expansion and the recorded uniform bound.
The corrected full remainder C+R+delta is positive and less than1 for x>=2.
The jump sign in C0180 concerns the explicit remainder, not an unspecified O(1) term.
The paired von Mangoldt formula and convergence are an explicit analytic input.

claims.claim: Landau's fixed-x zero-sum formula is a second explicit analytic input.
Integration by parts approximates each horizontal integral by x^rho/(rho log x) with a summable remainder.
The recorded zero-count estimate makes the total integration-by-parts error convergent.
Partial summation of Landau's formula yields the imaginary log T term at x=p^k.
Its coefficient is1/(2*pi*k), so the unpaired sum truly diverges.
Taking real parts of finite partial sums before the limit repairs C0179 without assuming RH.
Each Pocklington witness forces the full relevant prime power into its order modulo any divisor q of N.
Combining the order divisibilities gives f dividing q-1 without requiring a common primitive root.
The bound r<=f+1 gives N<(f+1)^2 and rules out a divisor q<=sqrt(N).
The empty-factor case f=1 permits only N=2 or3.
The prior certificate for n4 and its known factor45379 is reused.
The half-power congruence forces every prime divisor to be at least2^e+1.
The stated nonstrict k bound excludes a composite candidate by the square-root argument.
For a prime N>3 the reciprocity argument makes3 a nonresidue in the specified family.
The e=1 branch is handled separately; N=3 is the missing exception C0157.
The original k=5 exercise is covered for e>=2 and N=11 is checked directly.
The test uses e+O(1) modular operations rather than asserting identical measured timings.
Writing x^2=AF+B and A=kt+s gives the reduction B-t+sF.
That reduction lies between1-N and N-2, so one addition of N suffices.
For fixed small k, division of the high part is linear in its word length.
The known2003 correction from single-precision k to small k is incorporated.
For k=3, reciprocity explains the base5 cases and the divisibility-by5 rejection branch.
The fixed-single-word random search for a negative Jacobi symbol has no general termination guarantee in our proof.
